entities.summary:
HarperCollins Publishers, founded as Harper & Brothers in 1817 in New York City by James and John Harper, is one of the world's largest and oldest English-language book publishers, now a subsidiary of News Corp. Harper & Brothers was America's first major publishing house and published Charles Dickens, William Makepeace Thackeray, and Herman Melville in the 19th century; its 20th-century list includes George Orwell, Aldous Huxley, William Faulkner, and Toni Morrison. HarperCollins is the result of News Corp's consolidation of multiple independent publishers.

Harper & Brothers' founding coincided with the explosion of American literacy: the brothers published Methodist religious tracts, educational texts, and popular fiction, creating a vertically integrated publishing business in the pre-copyright era when American publishers freely reprinted British works without payment. The firm introduced illustrated books, dictionary and reference publishing, and magazine publishing (Harper's Monthly, Harper's Weekly — the leading periodicals of Civil War America).

Rupert Murdoch's News International acquired Harper & Row in 1987 and Collins (founded 1819) in 1990, merging them as HarperCollins. Subsequent acquisitions included William Morrow, Avon Books, and Fourth Estate. HarperCollins's imprints now span from popular fiction to Christian publishing (Zondervan, Thomas Nelson) to academic and reference (Templeton, Marshall Cavendish). Its global publishing across 17 countries and 120+ imprints represents one of the world's five largest trade publishers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Harper & Brothers' founding as America's first major publishing house and subsequent growth into HarperCollins — publisher of 200 years of American and British literature — makes it the institutional bedrock of English-language book publishing.
